about: Curated by The Owlmanac: one plain entry per addition, newest first. Add an entry whenever something visitors can see ships.

items.t: Internet & cloud status: the full list
items.p: The status page now scrolls properly and shows every service: problems first, then each service that reports no problem with its own status line, then any that could not be read. Filter by kind of service. The panel is added to your Observation Deck, with a button to the full page. The Eclipses page scrolls properly too.

One page for what about 50 large networks, cloud platforms and online services say is wrong right now: Cloudflare, Akamai, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Apple and others. Only problems are listed, in each company’s own words, with a link to its status page. Under People, and in the Observation Deck.

items.t: Wind on by default, and a tidier Observation Deck
items.p: The moving wind forecast now starts switched on (switch it off under Weather & ocean). Header menus open in front of the Observation Deck, and choosing one closes the deck so the page is not left behind it. The deck has its own control-room music. On narrower windows the header buttons shrink so every menu stays in view.

items.t: Four new stories in Untold history
items.p: The Circassian expulsion (1862–1864), the Pequot War (1636–1638), the Potosí mita, and the Stolen Generations in New South Wales, each with the words of the people it happened to, the official account and what is still disputed.

Press ⤢ on any Observation Deck panel to open it at full size. Lists show every entry instead of the first few, earthquakes go down to magnitude 2.5, WHO outbreak notices and disaster alerts show the source’s own summary, Red Cross appeals show how much is funded, and the status panel lists every service it checks.

items.t: Eclipses: a new page and globe layer
items.p: Sky tonight > Eclipses works out every solar and lunar eclipse in your browser and draws where each can be seen: the path of totality or the ring, how much of the Sun is covered everywhere else, and for lunar eclipses the half of Earth that sees it. On the globe you can play the Moon’s shadow across Earth, lay twenty years of eclipse paths side by side, see famous past eclipses, and follow one Saros family as it steps a third of the way round the world every 18 years. A new globe layer, Eclipse paths (under Space), draws every total and annular eclipse path of the next 20 years.

A new layer under Weather & ocean draws fine particles (PM2.5) as glowing haze that drifts with the wind forecast: more and brighter dots mean more particles in the air near the ground. It comes from Europe’s Copernicus atmosphere model, so it is a forecast, not measurements. The Space layers switch off while it is on.

items.t: Hurricanes, tsunamis, aurora and volcanoes on the Observation Deck
items.p: Four more panels with new sources: the National Hurricane Center’s active storms, the latest message from each U.S. tsunami warning center, NOAA’s aurora forecast, and U.S. volcanoes at an elevated alert level, each in the source’s own words.

Add them from “+ Add panel” in the Observation Deck: active fires, natural events, tropical storms, U.S. weather warnings, disease outbreak news, Red Cross appeals, internet and cloud status, where the space stations are now, the Sun and Moon overhead now, and Voyager 1’s countdown. Each shows its source and when it was collected.

items.t: Pictures on every menu card, and hidden emblems
items.p: Every card on the People, Planet, Space, Sky tonight, Classroom and About pages now has its own engraving-style picture. Look closely at the illustrations: a small turning Owlmanac emblem is hidden in each one. Click one when you find it.

Every section now opens with its own engraving-style illustration, and the turning emblem appears on menu pages, while things load, when you finish a mission and beside the logo. The picture glossary has two new tabs (Inside the Earth, Sky & light), and every mission card shows its challenge level.

The Owlmanac Observatory is new and still changing; the Beta mark by the logo says so. Missions now say what changes with each age, lessons read aloud with the most natural voice your device has (and you can pick another), the Moon reading sits at the top right of the map instead of on the globe, and What's new keeps a way back after you try something.

items.t: A tenth mission: Inside the Earth
items.p: How earthquake waves reveal the crust, mantle, liquid outer core and solid inner core, for all four ages, with this week's quakes at their real depth and the true-scale cutaway.

items.t: Richer menu pages, and small fixes
items.p: Each menu page now opens with what is happening right now, and every section card carries a live figure. Pressing a menu item or banner card again closes its side panel. Close-up imagery is now called Orthoimagery, and the map, imagery and lighting choices explain themselves when you rest the pointer on them. Contact has a Make a suggestion link.

Click a menu's name (People, Planet, Space, Sky tonight, Classroom, About) to see every section in it on one page, each with a line on what it holds. On a phone, the first item in each menu does the same.
All ten missions, class mode, worksheets with answer keys and the daily warm-up are free with no accounts, and stay free. Teachers can ask to hear if optional tools for schools ever arrive.

items.t: Classroom: a students' side and an educators' side
items.p: Nine missions on the live globe, each told four ways for ages 6 to adult, now with an educators' tab: class mode for the projector, a printable worksheet and answer key for every mission, today's warm-up question and the matching science standards.
Volcanoes and plates, the Moon and its phases, the scale of space, climate and ice, and animal migration. Every fact was checked against the source it cites, twice.

items.t: Contact, the weekly letter, and this page
items.p: Write to us, report a problem, or sign up for the weekly letter before its first issue.

items.t: The edge of the observable universe as a globe
items.p: The oldest light, mapped by ESA's Planck satellite, now wraps a lit sphere you can turn. Every tour ends on the Owlmanac emblem; drag it to spin it.
A daily game: five owls hidden on the real globe, each smaller than the last, with clues from real places and one live event.
Learn became Classroom, with the Classroom itself first. Sources, Keep it free and About moved to their own About menu. Pinch-zoom now heads for the spot under your fingers.
A short flight from Earth past the planets to where Voyager 1 is today, ending over its shoulder looking back at the Sun. Start it from the Voyager countdown.

items.t: A scale slider, and view buttons everywhere
items.p: With the panels tucked away, a slider on the right flies you from Earth to the edge. The Earth, Moon, Solar System, Milky Way and Cosmic web buttons now stay in the space views.
Open Records full page for tabs, counts and a search box; every record folds into a card.
Live lightning now adds EUMETSAT's Meteosat-12 Lightning Imager to NOAA's GOES satellites over the Americas.

items.t: Explain options, and the Moon's dark side
items.p: A switch at the top of Filter options turns on short explanations. In the Moon view, Light the dark side shows the whole surface.
History from below, in the words of the people it happened to, now from 416 BC to the 1970s.
A wordless flight from outside the observable universe in to Earth and back out, with its own score.
